html:
A vote in Australia on 27 May 1967 that changed the constitution so that Aboriginal people would be counted in the national census and the federal government could make laws for them. Over 90 percent voted yes, the largest yes vote in any Australian referendum.

The government of Harold Holt put the question after a ten year campaign by Indigenous and white activists, among them Faith Bandler. Two clauses were at stake. One left Aboriginal people out of population counts. The other said the Commonwealth could make special laws for people of any race except Aboriginal people, leaving them to the states. Both were changed.

The result is often remembered as giving Aboriginal people citizenship or the vote. It did neither: they were already citizens, and all had the federal vote from 1962. Its real weight was symbolic and practical. It showed broad public support for change, and it let Canberra act on land rights and welfare.

It came while children were still being taken in the Stolen Generations, and a generation before Eddie Mabo won native title in court.
